title: Futures and Forwards
objectives: Distinguish forwards (OTC, custom, settled at expiry) from futures (exchange, standardised, margined and marked to market daily)
Price a forward with the cost-of-carry relation, including financing, storage and income terms
Execute cash-and-carry and reverse arbitrage logic to identify mispriced forwards
Track a margin account through daily mark-to-market settlements
motivation: A forward contract lets two parties lock today the price of a trade that happens next year, the backbone of hedging for airlines, farmers and bond desks alike. Its 'fair' price is not an opinion about the future at all: it is fixed by an arbitrage argument with arithmetic precise enough to verify on one hand. Master the cost of carry here and every derivatives model later in the curriculum will feel inevitable.

blocks.md: A **forward** is a bilateral agreement to buy (long) or sell (short) an asset at a fixed **delivery price** on a fixed future date. Both sides are *obligated*, no premium changes hands at inception, and payoff arrives only at settlement. A **futures** contract is the exchange-traded sibling: standardised size, expiry and quality; a clearing house between the parties; and crucially, **daily mark-to-market**, gains and losses are settled into a margin account every day, not at expiry. Functionally they price alike; mechanically they differ in credit and liquidity.

blocks.text: Cost of carry: the fair price is a theorem

blocks.md: What *should* the delivery price be? Suppose you need the asset at date $T$ anyway. You have two routes: buy the forward today, or buy the asset today and carry it, paying financing on \$S of capital, storage $u$, and collecting any income $y$ the asset throws off while you hold it. Competition between the routes forces:

blocks.tex: F = S\,e^{(r + u - y)\,T} \qquad\text{(continuous)}\qquad F = S\,(1+r)^T + \text{storage} - \text{income}
blocks.caption: Cost of carry: financing plus storage minus income. No forecast of the future price appears anywhere.

blocks.title: Stock index forward: $S = 100$, $r = 5\%$, dividend yield $y = 2\%$, $T = 0.5$
items: Net carry rate: $r - y = 5\% - 2\% = 3\%$ per year.
Sense check: the stock is expected to pay dividends, so buying forward is *cheaper* than carrying, you forgo the income, so the forward price sits below pure financing growth.

blocks.text: Arbitrage: when the quote disagrees with the theorem

blocks.title: Gold, discrete terms: $S = \$1{,}800$/oz, $r = 4\%$, $T = 1$ year, no storage
items: Cash-and-carry (quote too high): suppose the forward is quoted at 1,885. Borrow 1,800 at 4%, buy gold, sell the forward. At expiry deliver gold, receive 1,885, repay $1{,}800 \times 1.04 = 1{,}872$. Riskless profit: $1{,}885 - 1{,}872 = \$13$/oz.

Reverse (quote too low): suppose the forward is quoted at 1,860. Short the gold for 1,800, invest at 4% (grows to 1,872), buy the forward. At expiry take delivery for 1,860 and return the borrowed gold. Riskless profit: $1{,}872 - 1{,}860 = \$12$/oz.
Conclusion: the no-arbitrage band is $F \in [1{,}872, 1{,}874]$ if carrying costs \$2 of storage, quotes outside it get arbitraged back, which is *why* the theorem holds in liquid markets.

blocks.title: Storage makes the band, not just the point
blocks.md: With no storage, any $F \ne 1872$ is money on the table. With \$2 storage payable only by the *holder*, buying forward beats carrying when $F < 1872$, while carrying beats buying forward when $F > 1874$. Storage (or large income, or lending frictions) turns a single fair price into a narrow no-arbitrage band, the width is the market's tolerance before arbitrageurs step in.

blocks.caption: Payoff of a long forward at delivery price 1,872: linear and symmetric, profit $S_T - 1{,}872$, no premium paid at inception, unlimited both ways. The short side is the mirror image: $1{,}872 - S_T$.

blocks.text: Marking to market: the futures cash-flow machine

blocks.md: Futures settle daily. Suppose you are long one 100-oz gold futures contract at 1,872 with an initial margin of \$4,000. The exchange settles against the *settlement price* each day, moving cash both ways:

Cumulative variation cash is \$200, exactly $(1{,}874, 1{,}872) \times 100$ - marking to market just *schedules* the same total PnL earlier. The operational consequence is **liquidity risk**: if losses drained the account below the maintenance margin (here, suppose \$3,000), you face a margin call and must top up or be liquidated, a forward holder with the same view and no margin system suffers nothing until expiry. At expiry, futures prices converge to the spot price by construction: the last settlement *is* the spot.

guidedExercise.prompt: An equity index stands at 4,000 with a 1% annual dividend yield; financing is available at 3% and the horizon is one quarter (T = 0.25). Compute the fair forward price, then state what a quoted forward of 4,040 implies and which arbitrage you would run.
hints: Compare the quote with the fair value before choosing a strategy.
guidedExercise.solution: Fair $F = 4{,}000 \times e^{0.005} = 4{,}000 \times 1.005013 = \textbf{4{,}020.05}$. A quote of 4,040 is 19.95 points too high → **cash-and-carry**: borrow 4,000 at 3%, buy the index basket, sell the forward at 4,040. At expiry: deliver for 4,040, repay $4{,}000 \times e^{0.0075} = 4{,}030.11$ (three months of 3% financing), keep the dividends $\approx 4{,}000 \times (e^{0.0025} - 1) = 10.01$ - net gain $\approx 4{,}040 + 10.01 - 4{,}030.11 \approx 19.90$ index points, riskless.

independentExercise.prompt: Copper trades at \$4.20/lb. Financing costs 5% simple for one year, storage is \$0.10/lb payable at delivery, and the 1-year forward is quoted at \$4.55. You can trade 25,000 lb. (a) Compute the fair forward price. (b) Design the arbitrage and compute profit per pound and total. (c) At what quoted forward would the arbitrage disappear?
hints: Fair = spot grown at financing + storage.
Cash-and-carry: borrow, buy, store, sell forward.
The no-arb upper bound is exactly the fair price with storage.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Fair $= 4.20 \times 1.05 + 0.10 = 4.41 + 0.10 = \textbf{\$4.51}$. (b) Quote 4.55 > 4.51 → cash-and-carry: borrow \$4.20 (repay 4.41), buy and store copper (cost 0.10), sell forward at 4.55. Profit $= 4.55 - 4.41 - 0.10 = \textbf{\$0.04/lb}$, so $25{,}000 \times 0.04 = \textbf{\$1{,}000}$ riskless. (c) The arbitrage vanishes once the quote equals the fair price, \$4.51 (below that, the reverse trade becomes attractive at prices under \$4.41, the no-storage carry).

commonMistakes: Pricing a forward as a forecast, the fair price contains no view of the future, only carry arithmetic.
Forgetting income the asset pays (dividends, coupons, lease rates): they *reduce* the forward price because the forward holder does not receive them.
Forgetting storage for physicals: it increases the forward price and widens the no-arbitrage band.
Simulating futures PnL as if it settled at expiry, daily margin calls can force liquidation long before a thesis plays out.
realWorldApplication: Airlines hedge jet fuel with forwards, farmers lock crop prices with futures, and the entire rate-hedging complex is built on forwards over the yield curve; margin engines process billions in daily variation payments.
quantFinanceApplication: Cost-of-carry is the first arbitrage argument every derivatives quant internalises; the same structure prices FX forwards (covered interest parity), equity index futures (basis trading) and commodity curves (contango/backwardation).
summary: Forwards are OTC, custom and settle once at expiry; futures are exchange-traded, standardised, cleared and marked to market daily.
Cost of carry: $F = S e^{(r+u-y)T}$ - financing plus storage minus income; the 5%/2% stock example gives $100 e^{0.015} = 101.51$.
Arbitrage enforces the theorem: gold at $S=1{,}800$, $r=4\%$ has fair $F = 1{,}872$; quotes at 1,885 or 1,860 earn \$13 or \$12/oz riskless.
Daily margining schedules the same total PnL earlier (long 100 oz at 1,872 → +\$200 by day 4) and adds liquidity risk via margin calls; futures converge to spot at expiry.

quiz.prompt: A stock trades at 50 with a 4% financing rate, no dividends, and a 1-year horizon. What is the fair 1-year forward price, in dollars?
What is the defining cash-flow difference between a forward and an exchange-traded futures contract?
options: Futures pay a premium at inception; forwards do not
Futures cannot be sold before expiry
Forwards are always more expensive than futures
Futures settle gains and losses daily via margin; forwards settle once at expiry
quiz.explanation: Daily mark-to-market through the margin account is the futures signature; forwards accumulate all PnL until the single expiry settlement. Neither instrument charges a premium at inception.

quiz.prompt: $S = 100$, $r = 5\%$, dividend yield $y = 3\%$, $T = 1$ year, continuous compounding. What is the fair forward price (to two decimals)?
Which changes *reduce* the fair forward price of an asset?
options: Income the asset pays while carried (dividends, lease income)
A shorter time to delivery, holding carry rates fixed
quiz.explanation: Income offsets carrying cost (subtract it); storage adds cost (add it). A shorter horizon shrinks the total carry exponent, pulling $F$ toward $S$.

quiz.explanation: $e^{0.015} = 1.015113$; the lesson's index example: 5% financing, 2% dividend yield, half a year → fair forward \$101.51.

quiz.prompt: Gold spot is 1,800, financing 4%, no storage. The 1-year forward is quoted at 1,885. Which trade captures the mispricing?
options: Buy both the forward and the gold
Sell the forward, borrow cash, buy the gold (cash-and-carry)
Nothing, the price difference is compensation for risk
Buy the forward, short the gold
quiz.explanation: Quote 1,885 exceeds fair 1,872 by 13: sell the expensive forward, buy the cheap asset with borrowed money, and lock $1{,}885 - 1{,}872 = \$13$/oz riskless.

flashcards.back: Forward: OTC, custom terms, one settlement at expiry. Futures: exchange-traded, standardised, cleared, marked to market daily via margin.
$F = S e^{(r+u-y)T}$: financing + storage − income. Gold at 1,800 with 4% financing for 1 year → fair $F = 1{,}872$.
Quote above fair: sell forward, borrow and buy the asset. Quote below fair: buy forward, short the asset and invest proceeds. Profits are riskless and grow with the gap.
